doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

title: Innovation, neoclassicism and Duke Ellington
summary: Innovators do not set out to innovate; time decides, as with Ellington.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yeah I believe so. And it seems like it’s an innovation in a sense when you’re bringing all those elements together because I’ve often wondered if it’s constantly getting harder for people to become innovators.

It’s a good question. Well it gets back again to industry stuff because you know in the 80s and 90s you had this term neoclassism thrown around a lot when it came to jazz. And they would often associate Wynton Marsalis with well he’s a neoclassicist because he’s playing in the style of Miles or the style of Louis or whatever. I mean now the musicians never thought, we never sat around talking, “Yeah you know what? I’m going to play something in the neoclassicist style.” You know? We never think that way. We’re simply trying to create music from what we’ve grown up with and to evolve as artists. And only time can take care of what is innovation and what is now. Louis Armstrong, Charlie Parker, Duke Ellington, none of them ever sat down and said you know what I’m going to be an innovator. Yeah, I’ll write something that will change the way people think about everything. I will play something that will change the way people play. None of them ever said that. They simply were pursuing their vision of music and art. I remember, there’s a great quote from Duke Ellington when he did not receive I think it was the

Nobel Peace Prize in 1969 or something like that. And when he was rejected for it and someone told him about it and Duke said, “Well I guess I wasn’t supposed to be too famous too soon. And here’s a guy who had been around for 50 years at that point and had already left an amazing legacy. And that just gives you a sense of where he was. He wasn’t thinking about accolades or accomplishments. And of course now we know him to be probably one of the greatest innovators if not the greatest of twentieth century music period. Of any category. And his music was beyond category. So yeah, I think if we stay true to ourselves as artists, as musicians, and as human beings, the innovation will come. Time will take care of that legacy. We have to just do what we do and let everything else take care of itself.
